Yes Bank reported a robust 65 per cent year-on-year jump in second quarter (Q2FY27) standalone net profit at ₹1,080 crore against ₹654 crore in the year ago period on the back of a healthy growth in net interest income and other income and decline in provisions.

In the interest of transparency in view of the recent Supreme Court decision upholding the Bombay High Court judgment and dismissing the appeal filed by the Bank relating to write down of Additional Tier 1 (AT1) Bonds aggregating  ₹8,415 crore, the Bank disclosed that assuming the estimated financial impact of the judgment had been recognised as at September 30, 2026, it would have incurred a loss of ₹5,217 crore in Q2FY27.

Further, the capital adequacy ratio - Basel III would remain unchanged, the annualised return on assets (average) would be negative at 4.3 per cent (proforma) against 0.9 per cent (not recognising the impact of the judgment) in Q2FY27.

Also, the net worth would decline to ₹46,970 crore (₹53,268 crore) and borrowings would increase to the tune of the re-instated bonds ( ₹8,415 crore) to ₹86.149 crore.

Vinay M. Tonse, Managing Director & CEO, Yes Bank,said, “Our Bank delivered another quarter of steady performance, with Net Profit growing 65 per cent year-on-year to  ₹1,080 crore, supported by healthy growth in core operating income and continued improvement in asset quality.”

“We respect the judgment of the Supreme Court relating to the Bank’s Additional Tier 1 Bonds. We are examining it in detail and will take appropriate steps in accordance with the applicable legal and regulatory requirements. We will keep our stakeholders informed as matters progress.”

The Bank said it is presently evaluating the consequential implications of the judgment, including the decisions and actions required to give effect to it, the manner and timing of implementation, and the resulting financial and accounting implications.

Yes Bank is also evaluating, in consultation with its legal advisers, all legal remedies available to it, including such further proceedings as may be maintainable before the Supreme Court.

“Pending completion of this evaluation and determination of the consequential actions and appropriate accounting treatment, the potential financial impact arising from the judgment has not been recognised in the books of account or incorporated in the reported financial results for the quarter and half year ended September 30, 2026,” the Bank said.

data.title: Should you subscribe to Zetwerk’s IPO?
data.description:
The IPO of Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses is open for subscription until Monday. The company, which runs a tech-based manufacturing platform, expects to raise ₹2,830 crore, while promoters and existing investors, including Peak XV, Accel and Lightspeed, are offering shares worth ₹2,182 crore through an offer-for-sale (OFS).

The promoter and promoter group stake, currently about 21 per cent, is expected to fall to 16 per cent after the IPO, before considering the dilution from ESOP shares. The company intends to pay down debt of ₹2,160 crore (out of ₹3,366 crore as of August 31, 2026) and use the remaining proceeds for acquisitions and general corporate purposes.

At the upper end of the IPO price band, Zetwerk is valued at an enterprise value of around ₹24,225 crore or at about 58x FY26 adjusted EBITDA. The eight-year-old start-up has no listed peers and is yet to become profitable.

Zetwerk operates at the intersection of two key areas of investor interest today — technology and manufacturing. It serves customers in sectors such as energy, consumer electronics, aerospace and precision engineering. However, considering the company’s profitability and the factors mentioned under ‘What doesn’t work’, the asking multiple looks expensive in our view. We recommend that investors give the IPO a pass for now and consider investing after listing, once they have greater conviction in the company’s execution capabilities.

What it does

Zetwerk serves companies operating in sectors such as utilities, renewables, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil & gas and AI (the ‘customers’). Its customers include marquee names such as Siemens Gamesa, Acer, boAt, CG Power, NTPC, Indian Oil, DRDO and the Indian Air Force. When a customer is in need of intermediate components/ inputs in the manufacturing process or is looking to outsource the manufacturing of certain components, it sends the order to Zetwerk.

At the other end, Zetwerk is connected to about 7,000 manufacturers (called third party suppliers), often MSMEs with low capacity utilisation and looking for scale. These third-party suppliers are capable of processes such as stamping, fabrication, machining, forging, die casting and assembling, and are spread across several countries including the US, Taiwan, Vietnam, Germany, Spain and Mexico, besides India.

Zetwerk now chooses an appropriate supplier(s) and sends the order to them for execution. Once the supplier is ready to deliver, Zetwerk purchases the goods from the supplier(s) and sells them to its customer. Contracts with customers are on principal-to-principal basis and Zetwerk is eventually accountable to deliver quality products as per the customer’s specifications. To ensure this, it deploys more than 2,250 operations staff at supplier facilities to coordinate production and supervise quality.

To complement the capacities of the suppliers in the network, Zetwerk has also built its own manufacturing facilities (both greenfield and acquired) for some processes such as assembling and finishing. Here, Zetwerk procures materials, employs labour and manages the process risk.

All these operations are managed through Zetwerk’s proprietary platform, Zetwerk OS, which covers the entire process — from order enquiries and supplier selection to quality assurance and logistics. Customers also get real-time visibility into order status.

These activities form Zetwerk’s first operating segment, ‘Manufacturing business’. The segment generated revenue of ₹9,375 crore in FY26, of which about a third came from its own manufacturing facilities (see chart for growth and margins). Products delivered include wind turbines, transformers, transmission switchgears, wires, cables, railway girders, washing machine motherboards, headsets, wearables and space antennae.

Zetwerk’s suppliers regularly use ferrous and non-ferrous metals and materials such as petrochemicals. The company negotiates bulk or repeat orders with large mills and manufacturers to secure lower prices. Leveraging this purchasing advantage, it has built a separate trading platform for these materials, selling them at a small markup (see chart for margin). Buyers include not only suppliers in Zetwerk’s network but also other businesses. Small-scale operators that may not otherwise benefit from bulk purchasing can also use the platform. This constitutes Zetwerk’s second operating segment, ‘Ecosystem business’.

Key business stats

Between FY24 and FY26, overall revenue has grown at a CAGR of 13.5 per cent, EBITDA at 293 per cent and adjusted EBITDA (adjusted for ESOP cost) at 108 per cent. Revenue from the core manufacturing segment has grown at a higher CAGR of 24 per cent.

Within manufacturing, energy products (solar modules, transformers, switchgears, wires, wind turbine nacelle sub-assembly, etc.), precision products (wearables, laptops, displays, PCBs, EV chargers, machined/ cast/ fabricated metal products, etc.) and capital goods (process equipment like reactors, tanks, steel structures, etc.) accounted for 69, 15 and 16 per cent of FY26 manufacturing revenue. These sub-segments have grown at CAGRs of 25, 55 and 5.5 per cent, over the same period.

Geographically, India, the US and the rest of the world have accounted for about 80, 18 and 2 per cent of FY24-26 overall revenue on average.

What works

Manufacturing revenue from repeat customers has improved from 78 per cent in FY24 to 80 per cent in FY26 and to 89 per cent in Q1 FY27. Net revenue retention rate stands at a median of 1.29x over FY24-26. This indicates that repeat customers have roughly given Zetwerk 29 per cent more business in the current year than the preceding year. These metrics show Zetwerk’s ability to consistently deliver on quality, especially given it works with the above marquee names.

New manufacturing order inflows were ₹15,393 in FY26, having grown at a CAGR of 31 per cent. Currently, the manufacturing order book stands at ₹13,062 crore or 1.4x FY26 manufacturing revenue.

Zetwerk gets both ‘built-to-print’ and ‘original design manufacturing (ODM)’ orders. ODM orders require Zetwerk to design the product on its own besides manufacturing it, while built-to-print orders do not. ODM orders typically have higher realisation. Share of ODM revenue has risen from 8 per cent in FY24 to 14 per cent in FY26.

Above all, the share of revenue from own manufacturing facilities is also on the rise — from 7 per cent in FY24 to 33 per cent in FY26. As captive manufacturing is a relatively recent initiative, rising scale of operations could create scope for margin expansion. Here’s how. When Zetwerk executes an order purely at the facilities of third-party suppliers, it purchase cost also includes the supplier’s margin. Producing the order at its own facilities, even partially, allows Zetwerk to retain some or all of that margin. The customer’s quoted price (Zetwerk’s selling price) remains the same in either case.

What doesn’t work

One, some of the company’s past decisions could raise concerns about its ability to execute and allocate capital effectively. Towards the end of FY26, it discontinued its third segment ‘Civil infrastructure works’, which involved building water pipelines and railway tracks, after the segment proved to be a drag on working capital.

The segment’s assets and liabilities are now classified as held for sale and are expected to be disposed by end of FY27. The segment’s net losses (attributable to equity owners) in FY24-FY26 were ₹65 crore, ₹156 crore and ₹642 crore, respectively, compared with losses of ₹854 crore, ₹210 crore and ₹991 crore, respectively, from the other two segments (continuing operations). However, the latter figure for FY26 was only about ₹195 crore after adjusting for a net-worth-neutral one-off item. For perspective, adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations stood at ₹97 crore, ₹323 crore and ₹421 crore over FY24-FY26.

Net exceptional losses from continuing operations in FY24-FY26 were ₹372 crore, ₹84 crore and ₹39 crore, respectively, after adjusting for the net-worth-neutral one-off item, taking the cumulative loss to ₹495 crore. Of the ₹616 crore in exceptional items, provisions for bad debts, supplier advances and unbilled revenue, impairment allowances and restructuring expenses accounted for a significant portion.

Management explained that most of these expenses related to the discontinued segment. Losses of this magnitude could have been avoided had management recognised the business’s working-capital-intensive nature before entering it. The prospectus also mentions an apparel trading business discontinued in FY24. An impairment loss of ₹62 crore against this investment is included in the ₹616 crore of exceptional items cited above.

Two, positive operating cash flows turned negative after accounting for working capital changes, in each of the three years. The trend continued into Q1 FY27.

Three, the business model allows room for leakages — meaning, some customers may try to bypass Zetwerk and send orders directly to the third-party suppliers. However, management’s defence is that the company can offer customers quotations competitive with market prices.

Four, the energy products sub-segment, which accounts for 69 per cent of manufacturing revenue, has gained significant momentum, with a revenue CAGR of 25 per cent, partly driven by the boom in AI-related capital expenditure. This growth could slow if sentiment around AI turns negative.

Five, auditors made several adverse observations in FY24 and FY25, including weaknesses in the internal audit system and the absence of a robust mechanism for physical inventory verification. They also cited ineffective internal controls over certain processes, potentially exposing revenue and receivables to misstatement risks. The absence of adverse remarks in FY26 and Q1 FY27 suggests that the company may have taken corrective action.

Overall, the company appears to have tried to clean up its books and present a couple of stable businesses to public shareholders, ahead of its IPO — which is a plus. However, the asking price appears particularly steep against this backdrop and a volatile equity market. Prudent, value-conscious investors may want a margin of safety against execution slip-ups, before considering the offer.

data.title: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 17 -- US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy.

Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously waiving several sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.

The order provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18, but suspends their application through a presidential waiver.

"Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the White House Executive Order stated.

The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn, while existing Russia-related sanctions under other Executive Orders remain unaffected.

According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), the decision provides India temporary relief but leaves open the possibility of Washington restoring tariff pressure during future trade negotiations.

In its report titled "U.S. Waives Russian-Oil Tariffs: Temporary Relief for India, but Uncertainty Remains," GTRI said, "For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty."

R Ramachandran, former Director (Refineries) at Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), told ANI that the immediate benefit for Indian oil companies would be greater crude sourcing flexibility rather than necessarily higher refining margins.

"So more than the GRM, what actually impact it will have on Indian refineries will be the availability of more crude choices," he said.

Gross refining margin (GRM) refers to the difference between the value of petroleum products produced by a refinery and the cost of crude oil processed.

Ramachandran explained that increased Russian crude availability could help refiners secure more economical supplies, depending on discounts. However, lower crude prices could also be accompanied by falling petroleum product prices, limiting gains in refining margins.

Rajani Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, said Russia's importance to India has increasingly shifted from discounted oil towards ensuring uninterrupted supplies.

"The discount has really reduced significantly. But yes, what is more important for India now is availability and ensuring consistent supply of crude oil for the economy," Sinha told ANI.

She said Russia's share of India's crude imports had exceeded 30 per cent in recent years, although its price advantage over international benchmarks had narrowed.

GTRI noted that Russia's share in India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as purchases shifted towards the United States and the United Arab Emirates.

The think tank also highlighted Washington's own energy requirements as a possible factor behind the waiver.

According to its report, the United States agreed to purchase Russian diesel under an October 9 agreement to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices.

It also noted that Washington had agreed not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that targeting India alone could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations.

"The message is clear: U.S. interests determine when penalties apply, while the ability to retaliate helps secure protection," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said in the report.

Meanwhile, Ramachandran said a sustained waiver could help reduce freight costs and ease logistical constraints associated with Russian oil shipments.

He said greater vessel availability and smoother payment arrangements could improve crude procurement economics.

"If Russia and India can agree upon on a continued ruble-rupee exchange for this, it also supports to ease the foreign exchange outgo which currently is affecting the Indian Rupee's strength," he said.

However, these benefits would depend on the restrictions that remain applicable.

On the broader economic impact, Sinha said India's current account deficit could remain manageable despite elevated crude prices, supported by merchandise and services exports.

She expects the current account deficit to remain between 0.8 and 1.2 per cent of GDP, assuming crude prices range between USD 80 and USD 100 per barrel during the remaining financial year.

However, persistently higher prices could widen the deficit towards 1.5 per cent of GDP under adverse conditions.

Sinha expects average inflation of around 5 to 5.5 per cent, although higher fuel costs and food inflation remain risks.

She said the fiscal impact would depend on whether elevated oil costs are absorbed through excise duty reductions, oil marketing companies or higher retail fuel prices.

Healthy tax collections and potential disinvestment receipts, including from IDBI Bank, could help the government manage fiscal pressures, she added.

On the rupee, Sinha said the waiver could improve market sentiment but was unlikely to provide substantial direct support to the currency.

She also stressed that a lasting India-US trade agreement would offer greater economic stability than temporary tariff relief, warning that fresh US tariff threats could emerge.

Ramachandran cautioned against immediately entering long-term Russian crude supply agreements without clarity on the waiver's duration.

"The first thing I would say is that it is too early to look at jumping into long-term contracts," he said.

He added that refiners would need to assess whether Russian crude discounts and stable supply conditions could be sustained.

GTRI similarly warned India against making permanent trade concessions in exchange for temporary relief.

"India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed U.S. pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," Srivastava said.

Arbitrum is increasingly pitching itself as a blockchain infrastructure business rather than simply another cryptocurrency ecosystem.

During institutional meetings reported on October 16, representatives discussed the network’s commercial potential with European banks, wealth managers and other professional investors. The participating organisations were said to represent more than €800 billion in assets under management.

Explaining The Business Behind The Blockchain

The discussions placed particular emphasis on how blockchain infrastructure can earn fees through licensing, network services and support for financial applications.

Research presented alongside WisdomTree material explored Arbitrum’s financial performance and the possibility of building sustainable revenue rather than relying on speculative token trading.

Institutional projects using Arbitrum technology are one possible route toward such a model. They demonstrate how a financial business might adopt blockchain infrastructure without requiring its customers to trade ARB directly.

Arbitrum’s community has also discussed new ways to generate revenue for its DAO treasury.

Interest Is Not Adoption

The meetings do not confirm that any participating bank has committed to deploy the technology, purchase tokens or establish a product.

For Arbitrum, the next task is converting conversations into actual commercial integrations. Banks will demand clear answers about reliability, compliance, privacy and the economics of using blockchain rails.

Still, the change in emphasis is notable. Blockchain companies increasingly want to be assessed on the value of the services they provide, not simply the price of their coins.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

data.title: Nine crypto firms form Quantum Alliance to set post-quantum standards
data.description:
Nine crypto organizations have teamed up to answer a question the industry has mostly been answering with marketing copy: what does "quantum-resistant" actually mean?

The group, called the Quantum Alliance, launched on October 15-16, 2026. Its stated mission is to define and test quantum-resistant standards for blockchain networks, and to make anyone claiming quantum resistance prove it against verifiable criteria.

The founding members include leaders from Quantus, American Fortress and Intmax, alongside other blockchain organizations that round out the group of nine.

The alliance says it will produce open definitions and standards for post-quantum readiness. The focus areas include transaction signatures and key management, the two places where a quantum attack would hurt most.

The work is split across four initial working groups:

Blockchain migration. How existing networks move from today's cryptography to quantum-resistant alternatives without breaking everything along the way.

Post-quantum zero-knowledge proof systems. Zero-knowledge proofs let someone prove a statement is true without revealing the underlying data. The group will look at versions of these systems built to survive quantum attacks.

Wallet and key security. Where user funds actually live, and where most of the practical risk sits.

Cross-chain compatibility. Making sure one chain's quantum fix does not leave it unable to talk to everyone else's.

The alliance has committed to publishing all of its outputs publicly.

Most existing blockchain networks rely on elliptic-curve signatures to prove who owns what. The concern is Shor's algorithm. Running on a sufficiently powerful future quantum computer, it could potentially work backward from a public key to the private key that controls the funds.

Blockchains are permanent records, and the public keys sitting on them are not going anywhere. An estimated 6.04 million to 6.4 million BTC, approximately 30.2% of the total supply, have public keys exposed at rest. Those coins sit at addresses where the public key is already visible on-chain, which is exactly the input a quantum attacker would need.

The broader cryptography world has already done some of the groundwork. NIST finalized its post-quantum cryptography standards in August 2024, giving governments and enterprises a set of approved algorithms to start migrating toward.

Blockchains, though, have problems that NIST's work does not neatly solve. Signatures get bigger with post-quantum schemes, which affects block space and fees. Migration requires coordination across thousands of independent users and node operators. And funds held by people who never move them cannot be upgraded on anyone's schedule but their own.

That is the gap the Quantum Alliance is targeting: taking general-purpose post-quantum standards and translating them into criteria that fit how blockchains actually work. The migration framework is aimed squarely at protecting vulnerable public keys like the ones holding those exposed Bitcoin balances.

For builders, open standards could lower the cost of doing this properly. A wallet developer or a bridge team would no longer have to design post-quantum security from scratch or guess what other chains will adopt. The cross-chain working group is especially relevant here, since a fragmented approach could leave assets safe on one network and exposed the moment they move to another.

For holders, coins sitting at addresses with exposed public keys carry a different long-term risk profile than coins that have never revealed their keys.

The founding roster also matters. The names publicly attached so far, Quantus, American Fortress and Intmax, are not the largest players in the industry. Whether the alliance becomes a reference point or remains a niche working group will likely depend on whether bigger networks, wallet providers and custodians decide to adopt or at least engage with its outputs.

data.title: ICICI Bank sees another margin squeeze in Q3 as FCNR-B costs kick in
data.description:
Mumbai, Oct. 17 -- ICICI Bank Ltd, India's second largest private-sector bank, expects its net interest margin (NIM) to dip marginally in the December quarter as the full cost of foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) deposits raised in the September quarter kicks in, before margins begin to recover.

"The full impact would largely get reflected in the third quarter, after which we expect the margins to start moving up, even based on the current level of policy rates," executive director Sandeep Batra said at a post-earnings press conference on Saturday.

The private lender's net interest margin (NIM)-the difference between a bank's earnings on loans and investments and its cost of deposits and borrowings-fell to 4.18% in the September quarter from 4.36% in the June quarter.

Its net interest income still grew 17.7% year-on-year to Rs.25,339 crore, and profit before tax rose 20.4% to Rs.19,724 crore. Excluding treasury, which posted a Rs.230 crore loss as government bond yields rose, profit before tax grew 23.4% to Rs.19,954 crore.

Batra attributed about 9-10 basis points (bps) of the margin decline to a change in the bank's deposit mix after it mobilized about $18 billion in FCNR-B deposits under the Reserve Bank of India's swap facility. Of this, about $10 billion was leveraged by the bank itself, about $3.6 billion came through partner banks, and about $4.6 billion came from retail depositors who took no leverage. One basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.

The inflows lifted total deposits 27.1% on-year, compared with 17% excluding FCNR-B, and pulled the average current and savings account ratio down to 35.8% from 38.1% in the June quarter.

Batra said the bank had done better than it initially expected under a scheme he described as meeting "an overall national need for foreign exchange".

The landed cost of these deposits, which is the all-in cost to the bank after paying interest to non-resident depositors and covering the expense of hedging the dollar funds against rupee swings, came to about 6.5%. That is slightly higher than the 6.30-6.40% the bank had estimated in their July post-earnings call, when the scheme was just launched.

The deposits run for three to five years and are exempt from reserve and priority-sector lending requirements, allowing the bank to lend the full amount. Part of the money has gone into repaying bulk deposits and funding loans, and the rest will be deployed over the next two quarters.

Total loans grew 30% on-year, or 24.1% excluding loans made by overseas branches against FCNR-B deposits. Domestic corporate loans rose 30.6%, which the management linked to capital expenditure, longer working capital cycles, a shift by companies from bond markets to bank borrowing and firms building liquidity buffers. The credit card book, however, shrank 9.7% on-year. They attributed this mainly to a high base, as festive spending began early last year, along with the bank's exit from customer segments it found unprofitable. "It is not a credit issue," Batra said.

The management said the bank's view is that RBI could raise the repo rate twice more by 25bps each, taking it to about 6%, while the central bank gradually withdraws surplus liquidity from the banking system. Since a large share of ICICI Bank's loans is linked to the repo rate, loan rates adjust faster than deposit rates in a hiking cycle, a pattern they expect to repeat this time.

The bank said the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India's (Irdai) consultation paper on distribution economics would have little effect on its earnings. The paper proposes capping commissions on single-premium life cover packaged with loans at 2% and describes such cover as "near mandatory in practice". That provision directly affects banks and non-banks that sell insurance alongside loans.

Batra said bancassurance fees account for less than 1% of the bank's total income and about 5% of its fee income, and that it sells insurance only from ICICI group companies. Asked whether its ties with group insurers would change if the paper is adopted as proposed, he said "nothing will change", adding that the impact on the bank's profit would be "absolutely minimal".

data.title: Nearly All Volume on FIFA-Linked Prediction Market Is Circular Trading — WSJ
data.description:
By Caitlin Ostroff and Katherine Long

ADI Predictstreet, a newcomer to prediction markets, made a high-profile debut during World Cup broadcasts after paying FIFA more than $150 million to become the global soccer organization's official partner.

Since late August, nearly every transaction on the platform has been made by a small network of linked accounts, according to an analysis of public data, suggesting that most of its trading volume is inauthentic.

About $108 million of the total $167 million in transactions that have been made on ADI Predictstreet through late September were made by cryptocurrency wallets that appear to be linked to the company, the data shows.

The accounts have almost exclusively traded with one another and are funded by a single cryptocurrency wallet that also collects the platform's trading fees, the data shows. Typically, trading fees are collected by wallets associated with a platform's owner.

ADI Predictstreet launched in April as part of a conglomerate led by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of Abu Dhabi's royal family known as the "spy sheikh," who serves as Abu Dhabi's deputy ruler and national security adviser for the United Arab Emirates. The company's deal with FIFA gave it exclusive advertising rights during 2026 World Cup matches. ADI Predictstreet aims to be "the world's leading prediction market platform, with millions of active users," according to the FIFA Museum's website.

ADI Predictstreet didn't respond to requests for comment. FIFA declined to comment.

The unusual trading patterns were identified by three Harvard University students — Joshua Gupta, William Thompson and Ashwin Vinod Kumar — who analyzed public blockchain data. The Wall Street Journal shared the students' analysis with experts who study unusual trading activity in cryptocurrency markets. These experts concluded that trading on the platform appeared to be inorganic.

"In this case, it looks like some of the trading fees are getting recycled back into the wallets doing the trading, and the only people who would have access to these funds are the platform themself," said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College. Crypto-tracking company Solidus Labs also verified the students' analysis.

Unusual trading began on the platform during the World Cup in early July. Two cryptocurrency wallets traded more than $81 million with each other across hundreds of different markets, some days amounting to more than 90% of trading volume on the platform. Both wallets were funded by an account that also collects trading fees for ADI Predictstreet.

After the World Cup, ADI Predictstreet's trading volume dropped significantly. Overall, roughly 26,000 wallets have ever traded on the platform, the data shows. But since late August, a network of 795 wallets — again all funded by the fee-collecting account — have accounted for 99% of the activity on the platform, the analysis showed.

"The retail activity looks almost dead," said Andre Guettler, a finance professor at Germany's Ulm University.

By late September, the most hotly traded market on ADI Predictstreet's platform was whether Democrat Ron Nirenberg, the former mayor of San Antonio, would win his race for Bexar County judge against Republican Patrick Von Dohlen. More than $650,000 appears to have been bet for or against Nirenberg, who the platform shows trading at 94% odds.

Every single trade in that market was made by one of the 795 company-linked wallets, the data shows, which traded among one another for roughly 10 days in September. The market has seen no trading since.

Nirenberg said in an interview that he hadn't previously heard of ADI Predictstreet. In general, prediction markets on elections worry him, he said. "My instinct says it's not helpful to our democracy." Von Dohlen echoed those sentiments, adding that he believes his odds are significantly better than the platform predicts. "It certainly is very problematic to have outside and foreign influence in United States elections," he said.

By comparison, combined trading volume on the much larger prediction markets Polymarket and Kalshi was less than $55,000 on the Bexar County contest as of Friday.

ADI Predictstreet is licensed by the gambling division of Gibraltar, which has embraced the moniker "Blockchain Rock" in trumpeting its openness to the crypto industry. In an interview Wednesday, Andrew Lyman, Gibraltar's gambling commissioner, said a preliminary review of the trading patterns surfaced by the Journal found ADI is in compliance with Gibraltar's regulations, which prohibit "self-trading."

"There has been no consumer detriment," Lyman said.

On Tuesday, after the Journal began asking Gibraltar's gambling division about Predictstreet, the ADI Foundation, Predictstreet's sister nonprofit, signed a memorandum with Gibraltar pledging to work with the territory on promoting cryptocurrencies.

ADI Predictstreet is listed in a June public filing as a subsidiary of the investment firm International Holding Company, whose chairman is Tahnoon. A company backed by Tahnoon also owns 49% of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, the Journal previously reported.

Shruti Choudhury, a spokeswoman for the investment firm, said it is "IHC's position that ADI Predictstreet is not a subsidiary of IHC." Choudhury didn't respond to additional questions.

Since last year, the ADI Foundation has also signed partnerships with companies including Visa, Mastercard, BlackRock, Franklin Templeton and Bank of New York Mellon to popularize the cryptocurrency blockchain on which the prediction market is based.

In late 2025, Ajay Bhatia, chief executive of ADI's parent company, agreed to pay about $170,000 to settle insider-trading allegations with India's securities regulator, pertaining to information he allegedly shared while CEO of another Tahnoon-backed company. Bhatia didn't respond to requests for comment.
